chapters.title: Chapter One — The Basement
paragraphs: Burgundy had been awake for thirty-one hours.
He could tell by the count blinking in  the corner of his monitor — the timer he set to motivate him. He did this. The number didn't bother him. The shake in his right hand did.

The basement smelled like smoking copper. Three monitors glowed green-on-black in front of him, lines of code scrolling so fast they made the dim room flicker. Cables ran along the floor in bundles thicker than his arm, taped down with whatever he'd had on hand — duct tape, electrical tape, in one place a strip of his own shirt. Against the far wall, beneath a tarp, the prototype waited.
He hadn't looked at it in six hours. That was on purpose. If he looked he'd find something to fix, and he didn't have time to fix anything else. Tomorrow was the day.

The monitor on the left was running a simulation of the drill's torque curve against twelve different ore hardness values, plotted in white-on-green. The monitor in the middle was showing the feedback gain table from the strain gauges, the numbers updating every few seconds as the simulation ran. The monitor on the right was open on a text editor, and in the editor, on the third line from the top of a function he had named GO, there was an off-by-one error he had been looking at for almost an hour without seeing.

He saw it now. He pressed the tab key. He pressed it again. He pressed it a third time and committed the fix and ran the simulation again and watched the torque curve resolve into something less ugly than it had been.
He let out a breath. An eye twitched.

Above him, somewhere, the palace was quiet. The palace was always quiet at this hour — even the kitchens, which started before dawn, had not yet started. Burgundy could hear the boiler in the next sublevel, a low irregular cough that had been part of the basement's soundtrack for so long that he no longer heard it unless he listened. He listened for a moment. Then he stopped listening and pressed his hands against his eyes and counted to ten.
He had been working on this thing for two years. This project no one understood. That he himself sometimes didn't understand. But he kept working.

Two years. Or — that was the official count. The number he gave himself when he was being honest about the project as a project. The truth was he had been working on something like the prototype since he was eight years old, when he had taken apart the desk clock in the receiving room and put it back together upside down on purpose to see if his father would notice. His father had not noticed for two months. When he had noticed, he had cuffed Burgundy on the side of the head and told him to leave the clock alone. Burgundy had taken it apart again that night and put it back the right way, and his father had never mentioned it again.
He thought, sometimes, about the miners. The people the planet ran on.  Their black faces and dying lungs.  The royals wouldn't have a cent to their name without their grueling work.

He did not know any of them well. He could not have. He was the prince, and the prince did not go into the mines except to stand at the rim during inspections, in the embroidered coat his father made him wear, while the foremen read from their clipboards and the King nodded at whatever they said and the miners below in the pits, black-faced, soaked through, holding their picks at their sides like rifles at parade, looked up at him without expression. He had been to the rim of the South 12 Shaft three times in his life. it was the "worst" mine. It wasn' just a pit, but a deep laberynth of tunnels. Burgundy's grandpa's guys found some special vein of ore down there. Never ending. So they just kept digging down.  it has become imfamous for how deep it went. a tangle of tunnels no single person knew the extent of. the elevators to get down to the deepest parts took 30 minutes one way. or so he heard from his uncle who used to sneak out as a teenager and explore. an active of royal rebellion.

Burgundy only knew the surface of South Twelve but remembered the smell. He remembered the way the work lights along the walls made the air look like it was full of something solid. He remembered one miner — a woman with a black face swinging her pick against a wall and directing the black crumbs that came off that wall into an impossibly old cart. Her sweat seemed permanent.
He thought about her, sometimes. A lot, actually.  in fact the entire thing he was building, a robot with a drill attached,  could trace back to her.  A machine that could replace that woman.

__________tktkkk He had not told anyone this. He was aware that it was the sort of thing that would sound stupid if he said it out loud — I built it for a woman whose name I do not know — and he was aware that this was also possibly true.
His father did not know about the basement.

Or — Burgundy hoped his father did not know about the basement. It was possible that he did. The King had a way of knowing things that he never said he knew, and then producing them in court like a magician producing a coin, weeks or months after he had first learned them, when the production would do the maximum harm. Burgundy had watched him do it to advisors. He had watched him do it to ministers. He had never watched him do it to family, but the family was small — just the three of them — and Burgundy had learned to assume his father knew everything until he had proof he didn't.

Still: the basement was his. It had been a wine cellar once, before some great-great-uncle had decided wine was beneath royal dignity. The bottles had been carried up and broken in the courtyard. Burgundy had read about this in one of the old palace ledgers,  He had taken the cellar over when he was twelve. He had run the cables down himself, through a vent shaft he had widened with a drill over a long summer. He had bought the first monitor with money he had saved by not eating lunch.
He had told himself, sometimes, that he was preparing for something.
He had not been sure, until tonight, what.
transition

The tribute ships came twice a year and he had watched them for as long as he could stand at a window. When he was very small he had asked his father what they loaded into the massive vessels. what were they taking away from our planet and what did we get in return? Everything, his father had said, in the voice he used when he was being patient. "Everything we have that someone else wants." he would say.  Burgundy stopped asking after a some years.

He had learned, eventually, the name of the man who wanted it. He had never met the man. Nobody on Dross had ever met the man. Nicholas was a name his father said the way other people talked about the season's rainfall, the rainfall that would affect the harvest— as a fact of the world that explained why anxiety ran high or low, why prices were what they were, why a miner who broke her leg in the South Twelfth Shaft did not get her stipend that month. It was all Nicolas.
Burgundy finished wiring up the robot's arm. he toggled his controllers to test it out. fluid and smooth. this was working. it would be impressive tomorrow
He had been careful in his rehearsals not to imagine his father's response.
His mother had given him a glance, at dinner.

That was all. A glance. She had not said anything to him during the meal — she rarely did, when his father was present — but at one point, when the King had been talking to one of his ministers about the southern tariff and Burgundy had been pushing food around his plate without eating it, she had looked at him across the table, briefly, and then looked away.

He did not know what the look meant. He never did, with her. He had spent his whole life noticing the things she did not say and trying to assemble them, and he had never quite managed it. Sometimes he thought she watched him the way you watch a clock you have built yourself, waiting to see whether it will keep time. Sometimes he thought she did not watch him at all and he was inventing it.
He was probably inventing it.

the code terminal blipped. The torque simulation had finished and produced an output graph he stared at for almost a minute before he understood what he was looking at. The graph was fine. The graph had been fine the last three times he had run it. He was running the simulation because he could not think of anything else to do, and he could not think of anything else to do because he was very tired.
He looked at his hand. Still shaking
He looked at the timer in the corner of the monitor. The number had ticked over to thirty-two.
He thought, I should sleep.
He thought, I cannot sleep.
He thought, I will not sleep.

He opened the editor again. He scrolled to the bottom of the GO function. He stared at the bottom of the GO function for a while. He moved the cursor up two lines. He moved it down again. He did not type anything.
The boiler coughed above
Somewhere far above him, the palace clock struck three.
He laid his head down on his arms.

He told himself it was only for a moment. He told himself he just needed his eyes to stop hurting. He told himself a few more things — small reasonable things, and then, between one of those things and the next, he was no longer telling himself anything at all.

The basement was dark and green and full of small mechanical noise, and the code flittered against his face like moths against a screen, and somewhere far above the palace, the planet kept turning toward the day he had spent two years preparing for, the day he had no way of knowing would not go the way he had rehearsed.

chapters.title: Chapter Two — The Court
paragraphs: The receiving hall of the palace was not beautiful. The King had spent his wealth on other things — huge statues, a collection of hunting portraits in a corridor no one used, a fountain in the courtyard that had not worked in years. droves of staff. The hall itself was tall and cold and made of grey stone the color of wet ash. There were no tapestries. There were no banners. At the far end, on a dais three steps high, sat the throne.
His father sat on it.
Burgundy had not planned to arrive late.

He had planned to wake at five, with an hour to wash and rehearse the pitch one more time and walk the prototype up the spiral stair without anyone seeing him. He had not planned to wake at seven, faceprint on his sleeve, the hours-counter showing thirty-five, his neck stiff in a way he could already tell would last all day. He had washed his hands and face in cold water from the basin in the basement. He had changed his shirt. He had pulled the tarp off the prototype and he had wheeled it up the stairs without speaking to it.

The doors of the receiving hall were always open during the council hour. Burgundy did not know if this was a tradition or a habit, but he had been walking past them his whole life. He had never walked through them carrying anything before.
He walked through them now.

The prototype rolled at his side on its single fat wheel. The wheel was loud against the stone. Burgundy had not noticed in the basement how loud it was. Down there the cables and the boiler had absorbed the sound; up here in the cold expanse of the hall the wheel sounded like someone dragging a coin across a slate.

The King was broad through the chest, his hair going silver at the temples. His eyes were the same color as the hall. When Burgundy had been very small he had thought his father was the largest thing in the world. He still thought so sometimes in dreams.

His mother stood beside the throne. Mira's hair was dust-grey, and she wore a gown the color of dried blood. She did not smile when she saw her son. Burgundy felt her watching him . He searched her face for the look she had given him at dinner the night before — the brief one, across the table — and he could not find it. She was looking at him a different way now. He did not have time to decide what way it was.

Three advisors stood at the foot of the dais — old men in old robes, the kind of men who had been advisors when Burgundy was born and would be advisors when Burgundy died. They watched without expression. The one in the middle had his hands folded as though preparing to receive something. The one on the right had a smear of ink on his collar he did not know was there. The one on the left looked at the prototype briefly and then away.
"You asked to see me," the King said.
"Yes, sir."
"This is the council hour."
"I know, sir."
"Then I assume you have something worth the council's time."

Burgundy stepped forward. The wheel was loud again. The prototype rolled with him into the open space at the foot of the dais and parked itself there as he had taught it to — a small command, hours of code, written for this single moment — and lit up. The panel on its chest pulsed green. It made a soft sound, almost like clearing its throat.
"Father," he said. "I want to show you something."
That was not what he had planned to say.  But the words came out anyway, and the prototype was already glowing, and there was no taking it back, so he kept going.

"It mines," he said. "Or it will, in the field. Twice as fast as a man with a pick. Maybe more, with proper tuning. I built it from scrap. The components cost less than a month's pay for a single miner. If we built a hundred —"
"Stop."
The King had not raised his voice. He did not need to.
"Father —"
"I said stop."
Burgundy stopped.

The hall was very quiet. The wheel of the prototype was no longer moving, and so the hall was, for the first time since Burgundy had entered it, fully silent. The advisors were looking at the floor. Mira was looking at Burgundy. The King was looking at the prototype as if it had crawled in on its own.
"What do you imagine you have built?" the King asked.
"A miner. A better one."
"And what do you imagine I will do with it?"
"Whatever you want. You're the King. You could —"
"I am the King." His father said it gently, almost patiently, the way one might explain a familiar fact to a young child. "And do you understand what that means?"
"It means —"
"It means I rule. Not metals. Not machines. Men. I rule men. I do not need to mine the mines faster. I need to rule the men who mine them. Do you understand the difference?"
Burgundy did not answer. His throat was too tight.
The King stood.

He was tall, and he came down the three steps slowly, his robe whispering on the stone and he stopped in front of the prototype. He looked at it for a long time. He did not touch it. He did not need to. The looking was enough.
Then he looked at his son.

"You think I haven't seen this before," he said. "You think you're the first person to bring a clever toy to a throne. There have been a hundred of you. A thousand. Every one of them believed he had discovered the thing that would change the world. Do you know what changes the world, Burgundy?"
"What."

The word came out smaller than he had wanted. He had practiced answering this question. He had practiced it in the basement until he had been able to say the word what with the right amount of dignity — but here, now, with the wheel silent and the green panel pulsing and his father a meter away and Mira's eyes on his back, the word came out the way it had come out of him at eight years old, holding a clock he had taken apart wrong.
"Will," the King said. "Will, and patience, and the willingness to do unpleasant things to men who are not as clever as they think they are."
His voice was almost kind. That was the part that was hardest.

"You are my son. You will rule one day. That is a craft. It is not learned in a basement. It is learned at my side. And you have not been at my side. You have been hiding in the dark, playing with wires, while I have been ruling. What I have given you is the only thing in this world worth having. And you bring me this?"
He kicked the prototype.

It was not a hard kick,  the prototype rocked back on its single fat wheel, and the green panel flickered, and somewhere along the right side of the hall one of the advisors made a small soft sound that might have been a laugh and might have been a cough.
Burgundy heard it.

In the basement, in the long hours of the night, he had run every scenario he could imagine for how this conversation might go. He had imagined the yes. He had imagined the no.  He had been careful — he remembered now being careful — not to imagine the laugh. He had not been able to bring himself to imagine the laugh.
But the laugh had not come from his father.

The laugh — or the cough; he would never know which — had come from an old man with ink on his collar, an old man whose name Burgundy was not sure he had ever known, an old man who had been standing in this room since before Burgundy was born and would be standing in it long after Burgundy stopped mattering.
"Take it away," the King said.
"Father —"

"Take it away, Burgundy. Do not bring it back. Do not bring me anything like it again. The next time I see you in this hall I want to see you in council robes. Listening. Learning. Not in overalls. Not with grease on your hands. Do you understand me?"
Burgundy looked down at the prototype.
"Yes, sir," he said.
He did not look at Mira.
He did not look at the advisors.

He turned the prototype around — by hand, because he did not trust himself to give it a command in a voice that would not crack — and he pushed it back toward the doors. The wheel was loud again. The hall behind him was silent. None of the guards moved to help. Burgundy walked the length of the hall with his hands on the prototype's housing and the green panel still flickering against his thigh, and at the doors he did not stop, and he did not look back, and he pushed through into the corridor.
The doors closed behind him.
He stood for a moment with his hand on the prototype, in the long cold corridor where his footsteps would have echoed if he had taken any. He stood very still.
The prototype hummed beside him. Its green panel pulsed once, gently — the loose connection finding itself again — and held steady.
He waited.

chapters.title: chapter 3 Mira's wing
paragraphs: The corridor stayed silent for the length of maybe a minute,  and then, muffled through the doors of the receiving hall, the council resumed. His father's voice came through as a low rumble without shape. One of the advisors was speaking. Then another. Then his father again, longer, and something that must have been a joke because it was answered with the soft polite noise a room makes when a king says something a room is required to find amusing.
Burgundy had been part of that room, before, from the side of it. He had never been outside of it, on the wrong side of the doors, listening in.
He listened.
He was still listening when the small side door in the corridor — a door he had walked past his whole life without registering — opened.
His mother slipped out.

She did not look at him. She closed the door behind her without a sound. She stood for a moment with her hand still on the handle, listening to the council, until the King said something else that was answered by the same polite noise, and then she turned to Burgundy, and she put one finger against her lips.
"Come," she whispered. It was less a word than a breath. "Bring it." her eyes dashing to the robot
Burgundy opened his mouth.
She shook her head — a single small motion — and turned, and began to walk.

He put his hand on the prototype's housing. He pressed the small command that told it to follow. The prototype rolled after him without being told which direction to go; he had built it with a tracking module keyed to his terminal and, since three weeks ago, to a small pin he had begun carrying in his overall pocket. Where the pin went, the prototype went. It was one of the things he had done at night when he could not sleep. He had built it because it was easier than steering.
They walked.

They took a corridor Burgundy knew — the long one that led past the council chamber toward the eastern courtyards — for about thirty paces. Then Mira turned right, into a smaller corridor Burgundy had walked twice in his life, and he began to lose his bearings.
She took him past a door he had believed was a broom closet. Behind the door was a narrow flight of stairs going down.
She started down them without hesitation.

Burgundy stopped at the top looking. The prototype stopped behind him. Its wheel — a single fat wheel, salvaged from a serving cart, rated for stone floors and stone floors only — was going to have to descend stairs.
He had prepared for this, sort of.

Two months ago, in the basement, he had cut the wheel open. He had lined the inner rim with a segmented rubber sleeve, and he had wired a small compressor into the prototype's chest cavity, and he had programmed a soft-mode that would let the sleeve slacken enough for the wheel to deform around the edges of steps. It had worked once, on a test stair he had built out of scrap in the corner of the basement. He had never taken it up or down a full flight. He had not been sure he would ever need to.
He pressed the command.

The prototype's chest made a small hydraulic sound. The wheel visibly relaxed,  it looked, for a moment, as though it had lost some air, and Burgundy pushed it against the first step. The wheel deformed. It caught. He pushed. The prototype rocked forward and down, awkward but functional, and mounted the first step, and then the second, and then a rhythm settled into it that was almost a walk.
Mira was three steps up, watching.
"You built this?" she asked quietly
"Yes."
She nodded once and kept climbing.
The stairs went up two flights. At the top, the walls changed.

Burgundy noticed it before he understood what he was noticing. The stone at the top of the stairs was a different color, warmer, cream instead of grey, and the sconces along the walls were made of a metal he could not immediately identify, worked with a pattern that looked, when he looked closely, like nothing he had seen anywhere else in the palace. The pattern was intricate and repeating. It looked like waves, or like maps. The air smelled different too. Not the wet-stone smell of the palace's lower halls. Something drier and older — books, mostly, and a faint mineral scent underneath that he could not place.
Mira did not stop to let him look.

She took him through a small anteroom and into a larger corridor with a high vaulted ceiling and windows on one side, all shuttered, all dusty. Their shoes made no sound; the floor here was carpeted, a long red runner going grey. Burgundy realized, walking down it, that the runner had not been walked on in months. Possibly years. Possibly he was the first person to walk on it who was not his mother in a very long time.
"Mother — where —"
"Not yet."

They passed doors. Most were closed. One was open a crack, and through it Burgundy caught a glimpse of a sitting room set up for guests who had never come — chairs still angled toward each other in conversation with no one. The whole wing had the feeling of a play that had been rehearsed once and then never performed.
They turned a corner. They turned another.
Mira stopped at a set of double doors, pushed them open, and stepped through.
The library.

Burgundy had known there was a library in the palace. There were several. The one near the entrance, where his father sometimes met with foreign envoys, had a wall of leather-bound treaties and a globe that had not been updated in his lifetime. The one off the council chamber held the ledgers and the tax records and the tribute receipts. Neither of them was this.
This library was three stories tall. bug deep into the basement

The shelves ran floor to ceiling on all four walls. There were ladders on brass rails that traveled the length of each wall. There was a spiral staircase in the center that went up to two levels of galleries. There were tables — long, dark, oiled tables — with reading lamps and stacked books and, on one of them, a small model of a star system Burgundy did not recognize. There was a globe. There were, so far as he could see at a glance, tens of thousands of books, and half of them were not in any language he had been taught to read.
He stopped.
The prototype rolled up beside him and stopped too, its wheel humming back to solid mode, its soft-mode air-cycle finishing with a small sigh.
Mira let him look for a moment. then he asked" Mother what is this place? Then she said, without turning:
"This is my library. This whole wing is mine. built at my request when I agreed to marry your father. My mother sent most of these books. this is a piece of my family"
"Your family," Burgundy said.
She turned.

For the first time since the corridor she smiled — a small, thin smile, without warmth, without unkindness either. The smile of someone acknowledging a fact that had been true for a long time before the other person had learned it.
"Yes," she said. "My family."

She crossed to a shelf on the eastern wall, second gallery up. She climbed the ladder without hurrying, and Burgundy followed her up because he did not know what else to do, and the prototype waited below on its wheel, its green panel pulsing slowly in the low light. At the top of the ladder Mira walked along the gallery to a specific shelf and stopped in front of it.
The books on the shelf were mostly grey and brown. A few had gold lettering.
One was yellow.
She reached up and put her hand on the yellow book — a plain yellow, no title on the spine — and she looked at Burgundy.
"This," she said, "was your grandfather's."
Then she pulled.

The book came out an inch, then stopped. Something inside the shelf clicked — a small mechanical sound, quiet but precise — and the whole bookcase shifted on some hidden hinge and began to swing inward, silently, like a great door on very old bearings that had been very carefully maintained.
Behind the bookcase was another room.
Burgundy had built rooms.

He had built the basement, over three years, from an old wine cellar. He had built the workshop in the eastern hills — the one Mira did not yet know about, or so he had assumed — from a sealed vent chamber. He had walked into his own rooms enough times to know what a workshop looked like when the person who used it had made it themselves, from what they had, in the dark.
This was not that.
The room behind the bookcase was white.

Actually gleaming white. The walls were paneled in some smooth pale material that was not stone and not wood and not metal exactly, but held light the way a page holds ink. Overhead — no torches, no oil lamps, no hanging bulbs — a row of long flat panels shed a clean cold light Burgundy had only seen once before in his life, in the receiving hangar where the tribute ships parked.
Along three of the four walls ran long white work tables.

The tables were clean. They were laid out with equipment. Not scrap. Not salvage. Real equipment: sealed processors in their original packaging, still bearing manufacturer's marks.; oscilloscopes newer than anything the palace had bought in his lifetime; a small array of green-glass panels stacked between wooden dividers; toolboxes with drawers labeled in a fine hand he recognized, after a moment, as his mother's.

Against the back wall stood a low shelf of documents — folders, ledgers, thin bound reports, all with the same neat spine tags. A stack of manifests. A stack of star charts. A stack of what looked, from where Burgundy stood, like schematics.
He did not step into the room.
Mira did. She walked to the nearest table and set her hand on it lightly, as though checking that it was still there.
"Come in," she said. "Bring it."
Burgundy stepped in.

He walked to the first table. He picked up a processor. He turned it over. It was a model he had read about in a manual six years old and had never, in the manual or in life, expected to see in his own hand. It was worth, at black market prices, more than a year of a miner's pay. There were twelve of them on this table alone.
He set it back down. His hand was shaking again, though not from tiredness this time.
"Mother," he said.
"Yes."
"What is this room."

Mira crossed to a chair near one of the tables and sat down. She sat the way she sat at council — straight-backed, hands folded — but her face was different than it was at council. She looked, for the first time Burgundy could remember, like a person and not like a queen.
"Your father does not know about this room," she said. "That is the first thing to understand."
"All right."
"Nobody in your father's line has ever known about this room. The Queen's wing was built with certain conditions attached. My family attached them. This is one of them."
"Your family?" Burgundy said again, because he still did not understand what she meant when she said it.
She looked at him.
"Sit down," she said.
He sat.
"You know that I was not from here," she said. "You know that your father married for the alliance. That is the version that is told at court. It is not exactly a lie. But It leaves things out."
"What does it leave out."
She considered the question. She considered it the way she considered questions from advisors — a full pause, the small tilt of the head, the calculation of what to give and what to keep.

"My family," she said, "is not a family in the way your father's family is. There is no title. There is no throne. There is no country. There is only a network. The network is very old and very large and it is spread across nine systems that I know of and possibly more. It moves things. Some of those things are legal in some places. Most of them are not legal anywhere. What we move most of, and what has kept us in business for the last two centuries, is minerals. Specifically the sort of minerals that are used to build the sort of processors you are holding."
Burgundy looked down at his hand. He had picked the processor up again without meaning to.

"Dross is not important to the empire. But Dross is very important to us. to my family. We move a great deal of what Dross produces. Not through the tribute channels — those are Nicholas's, and my family and Nicholas have an understanding — but through the other channels. The channels that do not appear on your father's ledgers.
She paused.

"Dross has been secretly trading with our people for years," she said, "they've always been able to find enough minerals in this planet to not only pay the tribute but also to sell to the shadow market.  But it was always full of mistrust. My people aren't just traders. they're pirates. they raid and steal and when your father's father wanted to formalize trade ties, my family offered a solution. The solution was a marriage, an alliance built on trade and trust. The marriage was me."
Burgundy could not think of anything to say.
"I was seventeen," Mira said

"I didn't have much of a choice, I was young, and even though I had dreams of my own I was the family bargaining chip, every generation has one. I knew I had to be sent here to this place. So I asked for the library. I asked for a whole wing to be built so I could continue my studies. My family agreed to fund it. Your father's family agreed to build it.
And in the 17 years since, I've been running a market of my own.
"A market?" Burgundy asked, still in shock at the unfolding world he had not known about.
"A market for high technology." she continued giving an air that she was sharing more than she had anticipated but was enjoying it.

" I have  secretly been buying items from far away systems using my families smuggling connections. Whenever a cargo vessel comes to collect minerals from Dross, I make sure they bring me the items I've requested. My cousin runs the Dross trade and has been very helpful"
"what do you buy?"
Mira gestured her right hand across the room indicating everything Burgundy was looking at
"All of this. High technology. Stuff your father hates but that I have always been fascinated with. Like you."
"{tk Mira says she seeeds this technology in the society to help people make their lives better and gives examples}

Burgundy tried to hold all of it at once and could not. His mother was a pirate. Not from another royal family like he had been told. her family ran A pirate cartel that raided ships, and moved blackmarket commodities around between 9 entire systems. In a sense she was royalty since a family that controlled that much trade would have to be extremely wealthy.

And here she was surrounded by gear, parts, and technology that Burgundy didn't even know existed. Stuff she had snuck onto the planet. 
Burgundy had spent two years thinking the basement was the one big secret in the house. But his secret had been one of two and his was the smaller one.
"how does father not know about any of this?"

"He believes that what I do here is read books and give instructions to servants who no longer exist. He has not been in this wing since our marriage. He has never opened the door to this library. He is not curious."
She said the last word — curious — with something like tenderness. It was the first tender thing Burgundy had heard her say all morning.
"why?" said Burgundy, looking at his mother like it was the first time
"why what?"
"why buy all of this?"

"I have always been a curious person. Curious about the world and fascinated by the magic that technology brings. My grand father lived through the advent of interstellar travel and when I was growing up he would tell me how much that changed everything. How entire systems were pulled out of poverty because now they could trade with huge empires across the stars."
There was a pause. and then Mira said,

"So I've been collecting all this. And more than collecting. A disc slipped into a servant's basket now and then, carried down to the quarters where someone might read it. A better pump sent to a village that had been hauling water by hand. Small things, quietly, for years. the people here dont know theve been cut off intentionally from the rest of the system.
and Waiting to see what you would become."
Burgundy did not know how to answer.
"Last night," she said, "at dinner. I looked at you across the table. Do you remember?"
"Yes."
"I had already decided. I decided a month ago that I was going to show you this room. Because I've been watching you in the basement"
"you know about the basement?"

"I have known about the basement for more than a year, Burgundy. I have known about the workshop in the eastern hills for eleven months. I have not intervened. I wanted to see how far you would take it on your own."
Burgundy said nothing.
"You brought it to him today" She continued" I knew you would. And I guessed the outcome. I told myself that if your father rejects it, it would be time to show you this."
They stood in silence. She walked to one of the tables. and picked up a spool of fine-gauge wire and turned it over in her fingers, once, and set it back down where it had been.
"I am going to offer you a bargain," she said. "Listen carefully. I am going to offer it once."
"All right."

"This room is yours. Everything in it. The processors. The tools. The panels. Whatever else you need, tell me, and I will get it.  You will not have to smuggle scrap out of the southern shaft anymore.  You will build here, in this room, with real materials, and a database of the most up to date knowledge and science. and you will build whatever you want to build. That is my offer."
She looked at him.
"In exchange," she said, "you will be the prince your father wants."
He looked at her.

"You will show up to council every morning, You will wear the coat. You will listen.  You will visit the mines with your father when he goes, and you will nod when he speaks, and you will smile the way he wants you to smile. You will be seen at the tribute inspections. You will attend the seasonal meeting with regional governors.  You will travel to the docks each month with him to see the tribute shipment goes smoothly. You will be, in every public detail, the son he wanted to have. If he calls on you to speak, you will speak, and you will say what he wants to hear. "
"He'll never believe it," Burgundy said.

"He will," Mira said. "He will believe it because he wants to. That is the thing about your father you have not yet understood. He does not see what is in front of him. He sees what he expects. Give him what he expects, and he will not look further. He will believe that the lecture he gave you after he shut down your prototype created a change of heart and that you've grown up, just like he always knew you would."
Burgundy sat with his hands in his lap. He did not look at the processors on the table. He looked at his mother.
"You are asking me to become him," he said.

"I am asking you to look like him. just to keep his eyes away from what you are doing here. if he finds out about this room and my support of you, it will end very poorly for all of us. Do we have a bargain?"
He thought about it.

He thought about his father kicking the prototype. He thought about the small sound the advisor with ink on his collar had made, the sound that might have been a laugh. He thought about the woman in the South 12 Shaft who had not looked up at him. He thought about the tribute ships coming down each month.
He thought about his father saying I rule men.
"Yes," he said. "We have a bargain."
Mira nodded once.
She crossed the room and picked up something from the far table — a small object he could not see clearly until she brought it to him — and she pressed it into his hand.
It was a processor. Not the one he had picked up first. A better one.
"Begin," she said.
She walked out through the swung-open bookcase, and she closed it behind her, and Burgundy was alone again.

chapters.title: chapter 4 The Double Life
paragraphs: From that morning on, Burgundy's life was never the same.

He began living two lives. Throwing himself into the work of being the perfect prince, and throwing himself even harder into the work he did when no one was watching. The first life happened in daylight, in halls, in coats. The second happened in a white room behind a yellow book and mostly atnight. For eight months, neither life knew about the other, and Burgundy carried both with increasing fear that his father was on to him.

but the more time passed  the more he realized mira was right. His father seemed to believe nothing was amiss. that believed the lecture had worked. the King saw the son he expected to see, the boy finally bent into shape, and he did not look further. Burgundy watched his father not look further, morning after morning, and filed it away.
He listened.

That was the thing about council that surprised him: how much there was to actually learn, once he stopped resenting the room. The kingdom he had grown up in and the kingdom that appeared in the ledgers were two different places, and council was where the second one lived.
He learned the tribute.

He had known about Nicholas his whole life but more like a child knows a fairtale. Now he learned the mechanics. The arrangement was old — older than his father, older than his grandfather. Nicholas provided security. That was the word the ministers used, security, always without irony, and it took Burgundy three months of listening to understand everything the word contained. Dross sat in a remote system, months of hard travel from the core lanes of the Universe Alliance. The Alliance's markets were real but distant; its protection was theoretical. A planet full of minerals with no fleet of its own was not a kingdom. It was a warehouse with the doors unlocked. Nicholas kept the doors locked. Nicholas's ships patrolled the approaches, and Nicholas's name — more than his ships — kept the raiders of six systems from descending on Dross. In exchange, Nicholas took the ore. Most of it. The royalty of Dross had resented the bargain for four generations and complied with it for four generations, because it worked, and because nothing else would. Every resource-rich planet in the region lived under some version of the same arrangement. It was not an alliance. It was extortion with a schedule. The ministers did not call it that. Burgundy learned not to call it that either, out loud.
He learned the mines.

Not the rim-of-the-shaft version he had been shown as a child,  the real accounting. Dross harvested eleven commercially significant minerals. Iron in bulk from the northern fields, where the seams ran shallow and wide. Copper and tin from the eastern hills. And from the deep shafts in the south,  the dangerous ones, the ones that took lives — the specialty ores, the ones that were worth shipping across systems: dense blue-black corvite, which was refined offworld into the substrate of every processor in the whole galaxy; threnite, which held a charge; pale veins of osmarine, which the ministers priced per gram. He learned that a single crate of refined corvite was worth more than a year of the northern fields' iron. He learned that the corvite in one of the processors on his mother's white tables had, in all likelihood, come out of the ground less than forty kilometers from where he sat — shipped offworld raw, refined in some distant system's foundries, assembled into components, sold to fuel the alliances advance computer systems but also onto the shadow market, smuggled back in by his mother's cousin, and set on a table sixty meters above the shaft it had been cut from, at a markup of roughly ten thousand percent.
Nobody on Dross could build a processor. That was the arrangement. That was the whole arrangement, seen from the right angle. Dross sold the flour and bought the bread.
He learned the army.

He had grown up thinking of the palace guard as the army. It was not. The army was three thousand men in barracks near the major shaft complexes, and it had not fought an external enemy in living memory, because external enemies were Nicholas's department. The army existed for domestic disputes. That was the ledger term: domestic disputes. It meant strikes. It meant slowdowns. It meant the year before Burgundy was born, when the southern shafts had refused to go down for eleven days and the army had gone into the workers' quarter and afterward the ledgers showed a one-time expense labeled pacification and repair. The army existed to keep the miners mining. Burgundy sat in council and watched his father review the army's budget with the same attention he gave the tribute, and understood that his father considered them the same expense. Both were the cost of keeping what you had.
He learned the festivals.

This was the lesson that stayed with him longest. Twice a year — at New Year's and at the midsummer Descent — the King opened the storehouses. Alcohol for every workers' quarter, paid from the royal accounts. Three days of suspended shifts. Music, lanterns, the great drum lines that Burgundy had heard from the palace walls his whole childhood, a low thunder rolling up from the city that he had always assumed was simply what joy sounded like. Millions of people lived on Dross in conditions that the ledgers, read honestly, described as slow grinding attrition — and twice a year the city below the palace erupted into celebration so bright and loud it could be seen from orbit, and Burgundy had grown up believing this proved something about the spirit of the place.
It did prove something. He just had the something wrong.

He was at his father's side, eight months in, reviewing the festival provision — the King signing off on the alcohol allotments line by line, generous, unhurried — when his father said, without looking up:
"Do you know why I pay for this?"
"No, sir."

"Because a man who has something to look forward to does not burn down what he has." His father signed the last line. "Remember that. It is cheaper than the army, and it works better. Men do not rebel in the weeks before a festival. They do not rebel in the weeks after, while they are still telling stories about it. Time it right and you are never more than a few weeks from safety." He set down the pen. "That is the craft. Nobody will teach it to you honestly but me."
Burgundy nodded the way he had learned to nod.

Some days, that was the hardest part of the whole performance — not the pretending, but the learning. His father was a careful ruler. That was the thing Burgundy had not expected. The cruelty was not stupidity; it was, as his father always said "craft", refined over generations, applied with patience. The festivals, the army, the tribute, the shaved stipends — it all fit together, it all worked, and his father moved through it with the fluency of a man who had genuinely mastered his inheritance. Burgundy sat at his left hand and nodded and learned the craft of ruling men, and told himself he was learning it as reconnaissance, and was never fully sure this was true.
The nights belonged to the white room.

He found his own ways up. That was the first project — before the hardware, before the discs. His mother's route through the broom-closet stair was hers; using it risked pattern, and pattern risked notice. So Burgundy went up instead of down. The palace's roots were deeper than its towers — old dungeon galleries, drainage vaults, dead corridors sealed and forgotten by men who had died before his grandfather was born — and the Queen's wing, he discovered, had been built onto a disused arm of that complex, its foundations grafted into the old cells. Over the first month he mapped three separate routes from the basement to his mother's wing, each surfacing through a different forgotten door. He took a different route each night. He never told Mira which ones. She never asked.
In the white room, he read.
The knowledge came on discs — and the discs, he came to understand, were the shape of the whole civilization.

There was no living connection between the stars. That was the fact underneath everything, the fact the Alliance's own maps politely minimized: information could be beamed between worlds, but a signal was months crossing what a ship crossed in weeks, decayed and stuttering by arrival. So knowledge moved the way freight moved — in batches, on hulls. The great relay stations of the core worlds gathered transmissions the way harbors gather cargo, wrote them onto discs, and the discs rode out along the trade lanes toward the periphery. A disc was a slab of pressed crystal the size of Burgundy's palm, dense with more text than the palace's three libraries combined, and by the time one reached Dross the research on it was a year old at minimum, often three. It did not matter. On Dross, three years behind the core was still fifty years ahead of anything else on the planet.

Mira's cousin brought them in with the cargo runs. Burgundy would slip his mother a written list — never spoken, always written, folded into the book she was reading at breakfast — and two or three months later a crate would arrive in the white room with the discs pressed between wool packing, labeled in a language he had begun teaching himself. Journals of the core-world academies. Engineering proceedings. Foundry specifications. And — the ones he read until the text swam — the code research.

The core worlds had a discipline for it. That was the revelation that reorganized his entire understanding of what he had been doing alone in a basement: whole academies, generations of researchers, devoted to the study of programs that improved themselves. He read papers on feedback architectures. He read papers on selection pressure applied to instruction sets, on programs bred like livestock across ten thousand generations in a single night, on the strange and apparently unresolved arguments about how far the technique could be pushed before the program's own goals drifted out from under its maker. Half the mathematics was beyond him. He built ladders to it — teaching himself, disc by disc, working backward through citations, filling notebooks with derivations until the notation stopped fighting him. He was seventeen and he was receiving, in batches, stale and secondhand, the education of a core-world engineer, and he took to it the way water takes to a downhill grade.
And he built.

The hardware changed everything at the pace hardware does — suddenly, in steps. The processors from Mira's tables ran his feedback code four hundred times faster than the salvaged board in his first prototype; simulations that had taken a night now took a minute, which meant he could be wrong four hundred times as often, which meant he learned four hundred times as fast. The crates brought hydraulics of a kind Dross's own industry had never seen — sealed actuators, compact and vicious, that could put three tons of pressure through a joint the size of his fist. They brought strain sensors finer than anything in the mines, servo assemblies, spun-carbon frame stock that weighed a third of the salvaged loader steel and flexed like it was human.
By the sixth month there were three prototypes.

They stood in a row along the white room's western wall, and they no longer looked like the machine his father had kicked. The single serving-cart wheel was gone; each unit now ran on a pair of independently driven treaded tracks that could soften or stiffen on command — his old sleeve-and-compressor trick, rebuilt with real components, so that the machines climbed the dungeon stairs behind him with a rocking, patient gait. Each carried twin drill arms on hydraulic mounts, a cutting head he had ground himself from offworld tool-stock, a sorting bucket slung between the tracks. In their chests, behind green glass, the processors ran his code. He had rebuilt the feedback architecture three times from what the discs taught him. The machines scored their own work now — depth of cut, energy spent per kilogram, waste ratio — and adjusted themselves within bounds he set.
They were, by any measure that had existed on Dross a year ago, marvels.

but They were not good enough, and he knew it. He had taught the machines to score themselves; he had not taught them to rewrite the scoring. Every real leap still had to come from his own hand on the terminal, and there was only one of him.

The practice wall was in the deepest room of his dungeon routes — an old cell gallery whose back wall, he had discovered in the second month, was not built stone but living rock: the palace's foundations sat directly on the shoulder of the southern ore country, and somewhere in the centuries the builders had simply cut into the hillside and called it a wall. Burgundy had sounded it out of habit, the way he sounded everything now, and the sensor mast had come back with a reading he made it repeat three times.
Corvite. A seam of it, thick as his torso, running diagonally through the rock like a vein of night.

It was, he understood, a small fortune sitting inside the palace's own foundations, unmined because unmapped, unmapped because no one had ever thought to sound the dungeons. It was also, more usefully, the perfect teacher. Corvite was the hardest ore on Dross — dense, brittle in the wrong ways, prone to shattering into worthless gravel if the cutting angle was wrong by even a few degrees. The southern shafts lost more men to corvite seams than to any other work. If the machines could learn corvite, they could mine anything on the planet.
So every night, after council, after the coat came off, Burgundy went down through the old galleries and set the three prototypes against the wall, and watched them try.

They were not failing, exactly. That was what made it hard. Each unit could bore into the seam. Each could strip freed ore into its bucket, sort waste rock by density, back out, and resume. Watching them work, a foreman from the southern shafts would have wept — three machines, no lungs to ruin, no stipends, no festivals required, chewing steadily into the hardest ore on the planet.

But steadily was the problem. The pace was wrong. He clocked them against the numbers he now knew from council: a good southern crew, twelve miners with picks and a blast allotment, pulled roughly a ton of raw corvite in a shift, losing a third of it to shatter. His three machines together managed perhaps half that, losing a quarter. Better per machine than a man. Not better enough. At this rate, replacing one shaft's crews would take three hundred machines, and he could build — with every disc and every crate and every stolen midnight hour — perhaps one every ten days.

And they did not improve the way he needed them to. That was the true wall, the one behind the rock. His feedback code let each machine tune itself — a better angle here, a smarter torque curve there — but the tuning flattened out. Each prototype would improve for a week, ten days, and then settle onto a plateau, grinding away at the seam with a competence that never became mastery. He would adjust the scoring, and the machine would climb a little, and plateau again. He was the bottleneck. Every real improvement still ran through him — his diagnosis, his rewrite, his upload — three machines waiting on one exhausted seventeen-year-old's judgment, and the seventeen-year-old was spending his days nodding at tribute ledgers.
Eight months. Three machines, and a plateau he could not code his way past.

Some nights he sat on the cold floor of the gallery with his back against the old cell bars, the notebooks piled beside him, the green panels pulsing their patient rhythm against the dark, and did the arithmetic again, as if it might come out differently. It never did. What he had built was remarkable. What he had built was insufficient. The distance between those two facts was where he lived now — day and night, coat and overalls, nodding and building — and he had begun to suspect, in the grey hours when the drum of the drills blurred into the sound of his own pulse, that no amount of his own cleverness would close it. He could not think fast enough for three machines.
